Why do we divide by √n to get the standard error — why not just n?
answer: It comes from the mathematics of variance. If you sum n independent values, the variance of the sum grows as n, not n². When you take the average, the variance becomes σ²/n, so the standard deviation of the average is σ/√n. Larger samples give more accurate estimates, which is why sampling distributions get skinnier as n grows. But the improvement follows the square root: doubling accuracy requires quadrupling n. Example with σ = 10: n = 4 gives SE = 5, n = 100 gives SE = 1, and n = 400 gives SE = 0.5.
